The Argentine toad Rhinella arenarum exhibits a maximum asymptotic snout-vent length of 13.1 centimeters [Li = 13.1 centimeters], a value derived from growth curve estimation across multiple populations. Heavy-bodied reproductively active females can attain an ultimate wet weight of 250 grams [Wwi = 250 grams], representing the largest adult mass recorded during field sampling efforts in the central Argentine pampas. The wet weight of an individual egg, measured from dissected gelatinous strings at site C2, averages approximately 0.018 grams [Ww0 = approximately 0.018 grams], though some bias is introduced by the hydrated jelly layers surrounding each ovum. Newly metamorphosed toadlets, by contrast, are remarkably diminutive, with a wet weight at metamorphic climax of just 0.2 grams . This thousand-fold increase between the egg stage and maximal adult body mass underscores the prodigious somatic growth potential characteristic of this bufonid species.

Laboratory incubation trials conducted at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C] revealed that embryonic development and hatching occur after an age at birth of approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days], a relatively brief period among neotropical anurans. The total length at metamorphosis, measured from freshly metamorphosed individuals maintained under standardized lab conditions, averages 2.4 centimeters . Wild-caught juveniles require about 60 days  since birth at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] to complete metamorphosis, with the first cohort of individuals finishing the larval-juvenile transition within this timeframe. The relatively extended larval period likely reflects the energetic demands of body plan reorganization, including tail resorption and limb bud development, which are strongly influenced by ambient thermal regimes.

Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, is attained roughly one year after hatching, with the time since birth at puberty measured as 365 days after hatching [tp = 365 days after hatching] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] in individuals reared under controlled thermal conditions. Females from the most productive populations reach an SVL at puberty of 11.2 centimeters [Lp = 11.2 centimeters], the largest such value recorded for any female in the study. This substantial size threshold before reproductive activation suggests that females must accumulate considerable somatic reserves prior to initiating the energetically expensive process of egg production, a pattern commonly observed in capital-breeding amphibians. Comparisons with congeneric species indicate that Rhinella arenarum delays maturation longer than smaller-bodied relatives, likely as a consequence of its larger ultimate body size.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Rhinella arenarum in the field is 5 years [am = 5 years] under environmental conditions averaging 23 °C [T = 23 °C], with the oldest individuals documented perishing primarily due to natural mortality during winter aestivation periods. This longevity is modest relative to other large toads, such as Rhinella marina, which can survive for over a decade in captivity. Annual survivorship appears to decline sharply after the third year, suggesting that reproductive senescence may limit lifetime reproductive output. The interplay between generation time and lifespan shapes the species' demography, with most reproductive effort concentrated in the first two to three breeding seasons following maturation. Inter-annual variation in rainfall and food availability further modulates survival rates across populations.

At the most productive site surveyed during this study (site C2), where the mean annual water temperature is 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output per female is substantial. Each female produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and that clutch contains approximately 34,535 eggs [N_R_i = clutch contains approximately 34,535 eggs]. This high fecundity compensates for the species' relatively low egg survival and high larval mortality in ephemeral ponds. The reproductive strategy thus emphasizes quantity over parental investment, with females allocating energy toward producing numerous small, jelly-coated eggs rather than fewer, larger offspring. Across all surveyed populations, site C2 consistently yielded the greatest clutch sizes, likely reflecting optimal thermal conditions and abundant aquatic food resources for pre-metamorphic larvae.
